Which two circuit quantities can never jump at a switching instant, and why?
column2: Capacitor voltage and inductor current: a jump would need infinite current (\(i = C\,dv/dt\)) or infinite voltage (\(v = L\,di/dt\)) — i.e., stored energy changing in zero time.

column1: DC steady-state models of C and L?
column2: Capacitor → open circuit; inductor → short circuit.

column1: Time constant of an RC circuit? Of an RL circuit?
column2: \(\tau = R_{Th}C\); \(\tau = L/R_{Th}\), with \(R_{Th}\) seen by the storage element (independent sources off).

column1: Why does a larger R speed up an RL transient but slow an RC one?
column2: In RL the resistor dissipates the inductor's energy (faster with larger R); in RC it throttles the charging current (slower with larger R).

column1: The master formula for any variable in a first-order circuit?
column2: \(x(t) = x(\infty) + [x(t_0^+) - x(\infty)]\,e^{-(t-t_0)/\tau}\) — same τ for every variable.

column1: How do you find the initial value of a NON-state variable (e.g., a resistor current) after switching?
column2: Draw the \(t_0^+\) circuit with C replaced by a voltage source \(v_C(t_0^+)\) (or L by a current source \(i_L(t_0^+)\)) and solve it.

column1: Percent complete after 1, 2, 3, 5 time constants?
50% delay of a first-order step response?
column2: \(\tau\ln 2 \approx 0.693\tau\).

column1: 10–90% rise time of a single pole, and its link to bandwidth?
column2: \(t_r = \tau\ln 9 \approx 2.2\tau = 0.35/f_{3dB}\).

column1: Settling time to within ε of final value?
column2: \(t = \tau\ln(1/\varepsilon)\); 0.1% takes 6.9τ.

column1: Settling time for an N-bit ADC (½ LSB, full-scale step)?
column2: \((N+1)\ln 2\cdot\tau\): 9.0τ at 12 bits, 11.8τ at 16 bits.

column1: Energy lost charging a capacitor from 0 to V through a resistor?
column2: ½CV² — exactly half of the CV² drawn from the source, independent of R.

column1: CMOS dynamic power formula and its origin?
column2: \(P = \alpha C V_{DD}^2 f\): each 0→1→0 cycle draws \(CV_{DD}^2\) from the supply regardless of transistor strength.

column1: How can you charge a capacitor with less than ½CV² loss?
column2: Charge it in N steps (loss CV²/2N) or with a slow ramp (adiabatic charging) so the resistor never sees a large voltage.

column1: Square-wave (0/V, 50% duty) steady state through an RC: \(V_{max}\), \(V_{min}\)?
column2: With \(\rho = e^{-T/2\tau}\): \(V_{max} = V/(1+\rho)\), \(V_{min} = V\rho/(1+\rho)\); ripple ≈ \(VT/(4\tau)\) when \(T \ll \tau\).

column1: General solution of \(\tau\dot x + x = u(t)\)?
column2: \(x(t) = x(0)e^{-t/\tau} + \frac{1}{\tau}\int_0^t e^{-(t-\lambda)/\tau}u(\lambda)\,d\lambda\) — an exponentially weighted average of past inputs (a convolution).

column1: Ramp response of a first-order low-pass in steady state?
column2: It tracks the ramp (slope m) delayed by τ, with constant error mτ.

column1: What happens when you interrupt an inductor's current with no flyback path?
column2: \(v = L\,di/dt\) grows as large as needed — switch arcs or transistor breaks down.

column1: Resistor vs diode flyback across an inductive load: tradeoff?
column2: Resistor: faster decay (τ = L/R) but switch sees supply + I₀R. Diode: switch sees supply + 0.7 V but slow decay (slower relay release).

column1: Ideal inverting op-amp integrator output?
column2: \(v_{out} = v_{out}(0) - \frac{1}{RC}\int v_{in}\,dt\); add \(R_f \parallel C\) (leaky integrator: τ = \(R_fC\), DC gain \(-R_f/R\)) to stop it drifting into the rail.

column1: kT/C noise at 300 K for 1 pF? Does it depend on R?
column2: ≈ 64 µV rms; no — it depends only on C (and T).

column1: The central tradeoff in an ADC sampling capacitor?
column2: Bigger C → lower kT/C noise but longer settling (τ = RC) → needs a stronger driver or more time.

column1: Why does on-chip wire delay grow with the square of length?
column2: Both R and C are proportional to length, so RC ∝ length²; repeaters break long wires into segments.

column1: Two equal capacitors, one at V₀, connected through R: final voltage and energy lost?
column2: \(V_0/2\) each; half the initial energy (\(\tfrac14 CV_0^2\)) is lost, independent of R.

column1: What does a negative Thevenin resistance seen by a capacitor mean?
column2: τ = R_Th·C is negative: the response grows as \(e^{+t/|\tau|}\) (positive feedback) until something saturates — the regenerative action of latches and comparators.

column1: Why can a bare resistor across a relay coil be a bad flyback design?
column2: It conducts the whole time the coil is energized, wasting power and loading the switch; put a diode in series with it (or use a diode + Zener).

column1: Capacitor and inductor element laws, both forms.
column2: i = C dv/dt and v(t) = v(t0) + (1/C)∫i dt; v = L di/dt and i(t) = i(t0) + (1/L)∫v dt (passive convention). Units: F = A·s/V, H = V·s/A.

column1: Stored energy in C and L, and average power in steady state.
column2: w = ½Cv², w = ½Li² (depends only on the present v or i). Over a periodic steady state the net energy absorbed is zero: ideal C and L have zero average power.

column1: What is continuous, and what can jump?
column2: v_C and i_L are continuous (finite power). i_C, v_L and every resistor quantity can jump. DC steady state: C is an open, L a short.

column1: Series and parallel C and L.
column2: C: parallel add, series reciprocal (like conductances). L: series add, parallel reciprocal (like resistors), if uncoupled. Capacitive divider: v1 = v·C2/(C1 + C2), the smaller C takes more voltage.

column1: Interrupting an inductor's current.
column2: v = L di/dt: 100 mH, 50 mA stopped in 1 µs gives 5000 V. Give the current a path (flyback diode, TVS/Zener clamp); the higher the clamp, the faster the release and the higher the switch voltage.

column1: Charge sharing between capacitors.
column2: Charge is conserved; energy is not: ½·C1C2/(C1 + C2)·ΔV² is lost, independent of the resistance (a smaller R gives a bigger, shorter pulse). Equal caps lose half.

column1: Volt-second balance.
column2: In periodic steady state the inductor's average voltage is zero (capacitor: average current zero). Buck converter: 8.7 V × D = 3.3 V × (1 − D) gives D = Vout/Vin.

column1: Real capacitor model and self-resonance.
column2: C in series with ESR and ESL, leakage R across C. f_SR = 1/(2π√(ESL·C)); above it the part is an inductor, so lower ESL (more parts, smaller packages, closer) helps, not more C.

column1: Decoupling a 1 A step: charge versus inductance.
column2: Charge: C ≥ ΔI·Δt/ΔV (1 A × 10 ns / 50 mV = 0.2 µF, easy). Spike: L·di/dt (0.5 nH × 1 A/ns = 0.5 V, hard) → many capacitors in parallel, plus package and die capacitance.

column1: Class I versus class II ceramics; inductor saturation.
column2: C0G/NP0: stable, small C. X5R/X7R: high C per volume but lose capacitance with DC bias, temperature and age. Inductors: above Isat the core saturates, L collapses and current runs away.

column1: Op-amp integrator and differentiator.
column2: Integrator (R in, C feedback): v_out = −(1/RC)∫v_in dt; drifts with offset. Differentiator (C in, R feedback): v_out = −RC dv_in/dt; amplifies noise. Triangle ↔ square.

column1: Practical op-amp differentiator: response to a step V?
column2: With \(R_s\) in series with the input C and \(R_f\) in feedback: \(v_{out} = -(R_f/R_s)V e^{-t/R_sC}\), a finite spike instead of an impulse, with the same area \(-R_fCV\). Gain for fast changes is capped at \(R_f/R_s\).

column1: Series vs parallel RLC: α and ω₀?
column2: Series: \(\alpha = R/(2L)\); parallel: \(\alpha = 1/(2RC)\); both \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}\). Same L–C pair, same natural frequency; only the damping differs.

column1: Characteristic impedance of an LC tank, and how it sets damping?
column2: \(Z_0 = \sqrt{L/C}\), peak voltage over peak current of the sloshing energy. Series: \(\zeta = R/(2Z_0)\); parallel: \(\zeta = Z_0/(2R)\). Critical: series R = 2Z₀, parallel R = Z₀/2.

column1: The two initial conditions of a second-order transient?
column2: \(x(0^+)\) and \(\dot x(0^+)\). Continuity gives \(v_C\), \(i_L\); slopes from the 0⁺ circuit: \(\dot v_C = i_C(0^+)/C\), \(\dot i_L = v_L(0^+)/L\).

column1: Underdamped master formula for any variable?
column2: \(x(t) = x(\infty) + e^{-\alpha t}\big(D\cos\omega_d t + \frac{\dot x(0^+) + \alpha D}{\omega_d}\sin\omega_d t\big)\), with \(D = x(0^+) - x(\infty)\).

column1: Series RLC hit by a step V from rest: peak current and worst-case peak voltage?
column2: Current peaks near \(V/Z_0\) (exactly \((V/Z_0)e^{-\zeta\arccos\zeta/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\)); \(v_C\) peaks below \(2V\), approaching 2V as ζ → 0.

column1: State-variable characteristic equation of a 2×2 circuit?
column2: \(s^2 - (\mathrm{tr}\,A)s + \det A = 0\): \(2\alpha = -\mathrm{tr}\,A\), \(\omega_0^2 = \det A\). Natural frequencies are the eigenvalues of A.

column1: Why can't a passive RC circuit ring?
column2: Coupling between capacitor nodes is symmetric, so for two capacitors \(bc \ge 0\) and the discriminant \((a-d)^2 + 4bc \ge 0\): real roots. Active circuits (dependent sources) can ring.

column1: When does the 02-03 overshoot formula apply in a circuit?
column2: Only to an all-pole variable responding to a step from rest (series RLC capacitor voltage, parallel RLC inductor current). Currents, inductor voltages and variables with zeros peak differently.

column1: RC snubber rule of thumb and its cost?
column2: \(R_d \approx Z_0\) of the parasitic tank, \(C_d\) ≈ 3–4× its capacitance (ζ ≈ 0.5). Loss up to \(C_dV^2f_{sw}\) (½ of that if an inductor's current charges it).

column1: Measuring a parasitic tank on the bench?
column2: Add known \(C_a\) and measure the ring frequency again: \(C = C_a/((f_1/f_2)^2 - 1)\), \(L = 1/((2\pi f_1)^2C)\). Halving the frequency means \(C_a = 3C\).

column1: Hot-plug overshoot: cause and cure?
column2: Cable inductance + low-ESR ceramic input = lightly damped series RLC: input rings toward 2× supply (more with Y5V ceramics). Cure: bulk electrolytic with ESR ≈ Z₀, an RC damper, or a TVS.

column1: Is the ringing on the scope real?
column2: A probe's ground lead (≈150 nH for 6 in) and tip capacitance form a tank ringing at ~125–140 MHz. Shorten the ground (spring): if the ring frequency moves, it was the probe.

column1: s-domain models of an inductor with initial current?
column2: Series: \(sL\) with a voltage source \(L\,i(0^-)\) (V·s, flux linkage) driving current in the direction of i. Parallel: \(sL\) with a current source \(i(0^-)/s\).

column1: s-domain models of a capacitor with initial voltage?
column2: Series: \(1/sC\) with a source \(v(0^-)/s\), + at the + terminal. Parallel: \(1/sC\) with a current source \(C\,v(0^-)\) (charge, A·s) pushing out of the + terminal.

column1: Where do a circuit's poles come from, and do they depend on the output?
column2: Roots of the determinant of the nodal (or mesh) matrix, the circuit's natural frequencies; the same for every input and output (apart from cancellations). Zeros depend on the input and output.

column1: Three structural sources of transfer-function zeros?
column2: A series branch with infinite impedance (parallel LC tank, series C at DC); a shunt branch with zero impedance (series LC, R + sL, capacitor ESR); two paths of opposite sign that cancel (Miller capacitance: RHP zero).

column1: What does a zero do to a step response?
column2: \(H = (1 + s/z)H_{ap}\) gives \(y = y_{ap} + y_{ap}'/z\): a LHP zero adds a scaled derivative (more overshoot, the more so near the origin); a RHP zero subtracts it (wrong-way start).

column1: ESR zero and why it mattered for LDOs?
column2: \(f_z = 1/(2\pi R_{ESR}C)\). Older PMOS/PNP LDOs used it to cancel a pole, so they needed ESR in a window (e.g. TPS760xx: ≥ 2.2 µF, 0.1–20 Ω); low-ESR ceramics push the zero too high. Newer LDOs put the zero inside.

column1: Can a passive RLC circuit be unstable?
column2: No: its stored energy can only fall, so all natural frequencies have Re s ≤ 0 (on the axis only for lossless LC loops). Dependent sources (gain) can push poles into the right half-plane.

column1: Stability test for s² + a₁s + a₀ and s³ + a₂s² + a₁s + a₀?
column2: Quadratic: \(a_1 > 0\) and \(a_0 > 0\). Cubic: all coefficients positive and \(a_2a_1 > a_0\) (Routh–Hurwitz, third order).

column1: Wien-bridge oscillator condition?
column2: Characteristic \(s^2 + (3 - K)\omega_0s + \omega_0^2 = 0\): oscillates at \(\omega_0 = 1/RC\) when the gain K = 3; above 3 it grows until amplitude limiting pulls K back to 3.

column1: Capacitors switched together with ideal wires: what does the s-domain say?
column2: A current impulse whose area is the transferred charge; voltages equalize at once; charge is conserved but energy is lost and the ideal model cannot say where (any resistance dissipates it). Dual: inductors forced into series conserve flux.

column1: Z = R + jX → Y = G + jB?
column2: \(G = R/(R^2 + X^2)\), \(B = -X/(R^2 + X^2)\). G ≠ 1/R unless X = 0; inductive Z (X > 0) has B < 0.

column1: Series ↔ parallel equivalent at one frequency?
column2: \(R_p = R_s(1 + Q^2)\), \(X_p = X_s(1 + 1/Q^2)\), \(Q = |X_s|/R_s\); for capacitors \(C_p = C_s/(1 + D^2)\). Valid at that frequency only.

column1: Dissipation factor D?
column2: \(D = \tan\delta = R/|X| = 1/Q\); for a capacitor with ESR, \(D = \omega C\,R_{ESR}\): losses grow with frequency.

column1: Why does an LCR meter have series and parallel modes?
column2: It measures one complex Z and must fit a two-element model to report C or L; Cs and Cp differ by 1 + D². Series mode suits low-impedance parts, parallel mode high-impedance ones.

column1: Circuit with a DC source and an AC source: method?
column2: Superposition by frequency: DC circuit (C open, L short) and the phasor circuit at ω separately, then add the time functions. Never add phasors of different frequencies.

column1: Voltage-drop approximation for a line R + jX feeding a load current I at lag θ?
column2: \(|\mathbf{V}_S| - V_L \approx I(R\cos\theta + X\sin\theta)\); valid when the drop is a few percent. Reactance matters only through reactive current.

column1: AC bridge balance condition and why two adjustments?
column2: \(Z_1Z_4 = Z_2Z_3\): one complex equation = two real conditions (e.g. Maxwell bridge: \(L_x = R_2R_3C_4\), \(R_x = R_2R_3/R_4\)).

column1: All-pass filter (1 − jωRC)/(1 + jωRC)?
column2: |H| = 1 at all frequencies; phase \(-2\arctan(\omega RC)\) (−90° at ω = 1/RC). Changes waveform shape and peak, not RMS or amplitude spectrum.

column1: What does a SPICE .ac analysis compute?
column2: Phasors: the complex nodal equations at each frequency, with nonlinear devices linearized at the DC operating point. No clipping, slewing or transients.

column1: When does phasor analysis fail?
column2: Transients, unstable circuits (no steady state), nonlinear elements (harmonics), and power (p = vi is not a phasor product).

column1: Instantaneous power of a sinusoidal load?
column2: \(p = \tfrac{V_mI_m}{2}\cos\theta + \tfrac{V_mI_m}{2}\cos(2\omega t + \theta_v + \theta_i)\): an average plus a double-frequency swing; P = ½VmIm cos θ.

column1: RMS of a sum of harmonics (plus DC)?
column2: Quadrature: \(X_{rms}^2 = X_0^2 + \sum X_{k,rms}^2\), because cross terms of different frequencies average to zero.

column1: Complex power?
column2: \(S = \mathbf{V}_{rms}\mathbf{I}_{rms}^* = \tfrac12\mathbf{V}\mathbf{I}^* = P + jQ\); |S| in VA, Q in var (inductive > 0). Complex powers of all elements sum to zero.

column1: Why does power factor matter if real power is the same?
column2: Current \(= P/(V\,\text{PF})\): line losses ∝ 1/PF², equipment rated in VA fills up, and utilities surcharge demand below a threshold (often PF 0.90).

column1: Capacitor for PF correction?
column2: \(C = P(\tan\theta_1 - \tan\theta_2)/(\omega V_{rms}^2)\); stop near 0.95 lagging — the last few percent cost disproportionately, and leading PF is no better.

column1: True power factor with harmonics?
column2: \(\text{PF} = \cos\phi_1 \cdot I_1/I_{rms} = \cos\phi_1/\sqrt{1 + \text{THD}^2}\): distortion lowers PF with no phase shift; capacitors cannot fix it, active PFC can.

column1: Maximum average power transfer?
column2: Conjugate match \(Z_L = Z_{Th}^*\): \(P_{max} = V_{Th,rms}^2/(4R_{Th})\), at 50% efficiency. Resistive-only load: \(R_L = |Z_{Th}|\).

column1: 80 PLUS power-factor floors (as of Nov 2026)?
column2: 115 V internal: PF ≥ 0.90 (Standard–Gold), ≥ 0.95 (Platinum–Ruby; Titanium/Ruby at 20% load). Redundant data-center Ruby: PF ≥ 0.96 from 20% load.
